1.3 The compression property


We next choose the projection operator {\mathbb{P}} and its range {\mathbf{W}}. The space {\mathbf{W}} needs to be large enough to contain the range of {\mathsf{C}}, but may also be larger. The central requirement that determines the choice of {\mathbf{W}} and the projection {\mathbb{P}} onto {\mathbf{W}} is the following ‘compression’ property.


Assumption 1.2 (Compression property of the heat bath).

There exists a linear operator {\mathbb{D}} on {\mathbf{W}} such that




{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}\big|_{\mathbf{W}}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}&t\geq 0\\
\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{D}}^{*}}&t\leq 0\end{cases}\qquad\text{on }{\mathbf{W}}.

(1.5)

The eigenvalues of {\mathbb{D}}+{\mathbb{D}}^{*} are strictly positive.



The left-hand side in the identity (1.5) should be interpreted
as follows. If we evolve the heat bath starting from w\in{\mathbf{W}}, the result
\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}w typically is not an element of {\mathbf{W}}. Then {\mathbb{P}} on the
left-hand side projects \mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}w back onto {\mathbf{W}}, as one does in
the Mori-Zwanzig framework. In particular, with the compression property the
flow map w\mapsto{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}w is equivalent to the memory-less
evolution \dot{w}=-{\mathbb{D}}w for t\geq 0.


Assumption 1.2 in fact implies that {\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}} is a
strictly dissipative semigroup, since




\big\lVert\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}w\big\rVert_{\mathbf{H}}\leq\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}\|w\|_{\mathbf{H}}\qquad\text{for all $t\geq 0$ and $w\in{\mathbf{W}}$},


where \alpha>0 is the smallest eigenvalue of ({\mathbb{D}}+{\mathbb{D}}^{*})/2.


Remark 1.3.

In Assumption 1.2, it is equivalent to assume only the
behavior for t\geq 0: the unitary nature of \mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}} then implies that
{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}={\mathbb{P}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}\right)^{*}{\mathbb{P}}=\left({\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}\right)^{*}=\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{D}}^{*}}{\mathbb{P}} for t\leq 0.
 ∎



The context of the compression property is the theory of (dilations and)
compressions. The relevant background is summarised in
Appendix C. In essence, the theory of dilations
states that for any contraction semigroup (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} one can find a
unitary group (S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} on a sufficiently larger Hilbert space such
that C_{t} is a ‘coarse-grained version’ of S_{t}. Conversely, one can in this
setting regard the dissipative semigroup as a compression of a given unitary
group. In our context, the unitary group is \mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}} and represents the
linear Hamiltonian system and \mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}} is the contraction semigroup. We
interpret a compression as a coarse-graining of a unitary group.


The crucial implication of the Compression Property 1.2 is that
the evolution \mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}} on {\mathbf{W}} is a semigroup. It is thus in particular
Markovian in the sense that the evolution equation does not involve the
past. In (2.5b), we give a representation of the heat bath
variable \eta which involves a memory term. The compression property allows
us to rewrite that memory term as a local term.


For the coupled system, the projection onto {\mathbf{W}}, i.e., the part of the heat
bath which interacts with System A, yields a compression semigroup. The
existence of a compression, and with it the associated compression subspace
{\mathbf{W}} is related to the theory of Markovian subspaces in linear systems
theory, see [LiP15, Ch. 10]. Necessary and sufficient conditions
for the existence of compression subspaces are given
in [Pic86, Th. 5.4]. We discuss the Compression
Property 1.2 in more detail in Section 3.


Example 1.4 (Running example, part 2).

Example 1.1 was chosen such that the unitary shift group
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}=\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}} admits an explicit and simple compression. We
choose a linear operator {\mathbb{D}} on {\mathbb{R}}^{3} with eigenvalues \vartheta_{1}>0 and
\vartheta_{2}\pm{\mathrm{i}}\varsigma with \vartheta_{2},\varsigma>0, and define the
functions f_{j}\colon{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{3} by




\displaystyle f_{1}(y)=\frac{\chi_{{}_{\leq}}\!(y)\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta_{1}y}}{\textstyle\sqrt{2\vartheta_{1}}}\!\left(\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}1\\
0\\
0\end{array}\right)\!,\ f_{2}(y)=\frac{\chi_{{}_{\leq}}\!(y)\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta_{2}y}}{\sqrt{2\vartheta_{2}}}\!\left(\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}0\\
\cos(\varsigma y)\\
\sin(\varsigma y)\end{array}\right)\!,\ f_{3}(y)=\frac{\chi_{{}_{\leq}}\!(y)\mathrm{e}^{\vartheta_{2}y}}{\sqrt{2\vartheta_{2}}}\!\left(\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}0\\
\!{-}\sin(\varsigma y)\\
\cos(\varsigma y)\end{array}\right)\!,


where \chi_{{}_{\leq}}=\bm{1}_{{]-\infty,0]}} is the indicator function
for the negative part of the real line. We then define {\mathbf{W}} to be the
three-dimensional subspace {\mathbf{W}}=\mathrm{span}\big\{f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}\big\}, and
the operator {\mathbb{P}} to be the orthogonal projection onto {\mathbf{W}}. Note that
\{f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}\} forms an orthonormal basis of {\mathbf{W}}\subset{\mathbf{H}}.


The validity of the compression property can roughly be seen as follows:
For t>0 the functions {\mathbb{S}}_{t}f_{j}=f_{j}(\,\cdot\,{-}t) immediately leave
{\mathbf{W}}, but they return to {\mathbf{W}}, if we cut them off at y=0 by multiplying
with \chi_{{}_{\leq}}, i.e. \chi_{{}_{\leq}}{\mathbb{S}}_{t}f_{j}\in{\mathbf{W}}. Moreover, we can express
this action by the contraction semigroup \mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}, see the calculations in
the proof of Proposition C.4.


Using the orthonormal basis \{f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}\} we can identify {\mathbf{W}} with {\mathbb{R}}^{3}
and using the orthogonal projections {\mathbb{P}} from {\mathbf{H}} to {\mathbf{W}} we find





\displaystyle{\mathbb{D}}=\begin{pmatrix}\vartheta_{1}&0&0\\
0&\vartheta_{2}&-\varsigma\\
0&\varsigma&\vartheta_{2}\end{pmatrix}\ \text{ and }




\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}\big|_{\mathbf{W}}=\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta_{1}t}&0&0\\
0&\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta_{2}t}\cos(\varsigma t)&\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta_{2}t}\sin(\varsigma t)\\
0&-\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta_{2}t}\sin(\varsigma t)&\mathrm{e}^{-\vartheta_{2}t}\cos(\varsigma t)\end{pmatrix}\text{ for }t\geq 0.




Having the explicit representation of {\mathbf{W}}, the coupling
\mathsf{C}\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\to{\mathbf{W}}\subset{\mathbf{H}} can be specified as
\mathsf{C}q=(\mathsf{c}^{1}{\cdot}q)f_{1}+(\mathsf{c}^{2}{\cdot}q)f_{2}+(\mathsf{c}^{3}{\cdot}q)f_{3},
where \mathsf{c}^{1},\mathsf{c}^{2},\mathsf{c}^{3}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n} are given coupling vectors. Hence,
the coupling energy reads




{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{C}}(q,p,\eta)=\left(\mathsf{C}q\middle|{\mathbb{P}}\eta\right)_{\mathbf{H}}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}(\mathsf{c}^{j}{\cdot}q)\int_{-\infty}^{0}\!\!f_{j}(x){\cdot}\eta(x)\;\!\mathrm{d}x,


and the coupled ODE-PDE system takes the explicit form




\frac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}t}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}q\\
p\\[3.00003pt]
\eta\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}p\\
\!\!-{\mathrm{D}}V(q)-\sum_{1}^{3}\int_{-\infty}^{0}f_{j}(y){\cdot}\eta(y)\;\!\mathrm{d}y\;\mathsf{c}^{j}\\[3.00003pt]
-\partial_{x}\big(\eta+\sum_{1}^{3}(\mathsf{c}^{j}{\cdot}q)f_{j}(\cdot)\big)\end{array}\right).


We see that the coupling between the ODEs (first two equations) and the linear
transport equation (third equation) occurs through the observable
functions f_{j}\in{\mathbf{W}}, which are exponentially decaying.


As mentioned above, the transport equation has to be interpreted in a suitable
weak or mild form if we want to treat general initial conditions. Note also
that the functions f_{j} do not lie in the domain of the generator {\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}} of
the unitary group \mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}, because \mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}})={\mathrm{H}}^{1}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbb{R}}^{3})
and hence {\mathbf{W}}\cap\mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}})=\{0\}.

3.1 Compressions and dilations


The theory of dilations, developed in the 1950s by Béla Sz.-Nagy and
Foias [Sz.53, SzF70], provides an embedding of a strongly
continuous semigroup in a unitary group. This can be interpreted as the
embedding of irreversible dynamics in reversible dynamics on a larger space,
such that the irreversible dynamics can be obtained by projection to a
subspace. For us, the ‘reverse’ procedure is of interest, namely the
compression of a unitary group to a contraction semigroup.


While for coarse-graining compressions are the natural concept, the theory of dilations provides crucial
motivation for the choice of the model discussed in this paper. For a given strongly continuous contraction
semigroup (thought of as a large-scale, thermodynamic description), the theory of dilations provides the
existence of a unitary semigroup which is unique up to isomorphism, and has a representation as time shift in
a suitable space (the theory of dilations is closely related to one-dimensional scattering theory, cf. [LaS89, Cha. III.2]). We give an explicit construction of this dilation in
Appendix C.


An important aspect of this specific construction is that it can simulaneously
be used to define the larger space {\mathbf{X}} and the extension of the unitary
group (\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} on {\mathbf{H}} to a strongly continuous
group (\widehat{S}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} on the space {\mathbf{X}}, as required by
Assumption 2.3.


Definition 3.1 (Contractions, dilations and compressions).

A strongly continuous semigroup (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} of bounded linear operators
on a Hilbert space {\mathbf{G}} is called a contraction semigroup if
\|C_{t}z\|\leq\|z\| for all t\geq 0 and z\in{\mathbf{G}}.


A dilation of the contraction semigroup (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} on {\mathbf{G}}
is a pair \big({\mathbf{H}},(S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) of a Hilbert
space {\mathbf{H}} that contains {\mathbf{G}} as a closed subspace (with the same
scalar product) and a strongly
continuous unitary group (S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} such that




{\mathbb{P}}S_{t}\big|_{\mathbf{G}}=C_{t}\in\mathrm{Lin}({\mathbf{G}};{\mathbf{G}})\quad\text{for all }t\geq 0,


where {\mathbb{P}}\colon{\mathbf{H}}\to{\mathbf{G}}\subset{\mathbf{H}} is the orthogonal projection of
{\mathbf{H}} onto {\mathbf{G}}. In this case, (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} is called a
compression of the group (S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}.



Every contraction semigroup has a dilation; however, one cannot expect a
general unitary group to have a compression. We come back to this point in
Appendix C.


In light of this definition, the important Compression Property 1.2 states that the evolution
of the heat bath can be compressed to a contraction semigroup C_{t}=\mathrm{e}^{-{\mathbb{D}}t}. With the additional
structure of Assumption 1.2 we can say much more about the process
Y_{t}(\eta_{0}):=\widehat{\mathbb{P}}\widehat{S}_{t}\eta_{0} than in Lemma 2.4:


Lemma 3.2.

Under the same assumptions as Lemma 2.4, and in addition
Assumption 1.2, t\mapsto Y_{t}(\eta_{0}) is a stationary {\mathbf{W}}-valued
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with drift -{\mathbb{D}}Y and mobility \Sigma
satisfying \Sigma\Sigma^{*}=\tfrac{1}{\beta}({\mathbb{D}}+{\mathbb{D}}^{*}).


That is, Y_{t}=Y_{t}(\eta_{0}) is a stationary solution of the stochastic differential equation




{\mathrm{d}}Y_{t}+{\mathbb{D}}Y_{t}{\mathrm{d}}t=\Sigma\;\!\mathrm{d}B_{t},

(3.1)

where B is a standard {\mathbf{W}}-valued Brownian motion. The process Y has
covariance matrix




{\mathbb{E}}Y_{t}{\otimes}Y_{s}={\mathbf{R}}(s,t):=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\beta}\mathrm{e}^{-(t-s){\mathbb{D}}}&\text{for }t\geq s,\\
\frac{1}{\beta}\mathrm{e}^{-(s-t){\mathbb{D}}^{*}}&\text{for }t\leq s.\end{cases}


In particular, Y_{t} is a Gaussian process with continuous sample paths.


Similarly, if \xi_{0}\sim\widehat{\mathbb{Q}}_{\#}\gamma_{\beta}, then Y(\xi_{0}) is a
(non-stationary) Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process satisfying (3.1) and
Y_{0}(\xi_{0})=0 almost surely.



Proof.

For any t_{1},\dots,t_{n}\in{\mathbb{R}}, the vector
(Y_{t_{1}}(\eta_{0}),\dots,Y_{t_{n}}(\eta_{0}))\in{\mathbf{W}}^{n} consists of n
measurable linear maps applied the Gaussian random variable \eta_{0}, and
therefore is a multivariate Gaussian random variable. This means that the
process t\mapsto Y_{t}(\eta_{0}) is a Gaussian process. Since \eta_{0} is
centered, Y_{t} also is centered, and since t\mapsto\widehat{S}_{t}\eta_{0} is
stationary, the same holds for Y_{t}.


We calculate the covariance function of Y_{t}(\eta_{0}) for
\eta_{0}\sim\gamma_{\beta}. First remark that by the Compression
Property 1.2




{\mathbf{R}}(s,t)=\frac{1}{\beta}{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{(t-s){\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}.


For fixed h_{1},h_{2}\in{\mathbf{H}} and s,t\in{\mathbb{R}} we then calculate the expectation
with respect to \eta_{0},





\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\left(Y_{t}\middle|h_{1}\right)_{H}\left(Y_{s}\middle|h_{2}\right)_{H}={\mathbb{E}}\left(\widehat{\mathbb{P}}\widehat{S}_{t}\eta_{0}\middle|h_{1}\right)_{H}\left(\widehat{\mathbb{P}}\widehat{S}_{s}\eta_{0}\middle|h_{2}\right)_{H}={\mathbb{E}}\left(\eta_{0}\middle|\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}h_{1}\right)_{H}\left(\eta_{0}\middle|\mathrm{e}^{-s{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}h_{2}\right)_{H}




\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt\kern-40.15991pt\mathrel{\mathop{=}\limits^{\eqref{eq:formula-for-covariance}}}\frac{1}{\beta}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}h_{1}\middle|\mathrm{e}^{-s{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}h_{2}\right)_{H}=\frac{1}{\beta}\left(h_{1}\middle|{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{(t-s){\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\mathbb{P}}h_{2}\right)_{H}=\left(h_{1}\middle|{\mathbf{R}}(s,t)h_{2}\right)_{H}.


Therefore Y is a stationary centered Gaussian process with covariance
matrix {\mathbf{R}}(s,t); this property characterizes the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
process with drift -{\mathbb{D}}Y and mobility \Sigma.22

If \xi_{0}\sim\widehat{\mathbb{Q}}_{\#}\gamma_{\beta}, then by choosing w_{0}\in{\mathbf{W}} randomly according to \widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\#}\gamma_{\beta}, the sum \eta_{0}:=w_{0}+\xi_{0} is distributed according to \gamma_{\beta} (see Lemma A.7), and the remarks above apply.
Writing for t\geq 0




Y_{t}(\xi_{0})=Y_{t}(\eta_{0})-Y_{t}(w_{0})=Y_{t}(\eta_{0})-{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}w_{0}=Y_{t}(\eta_{0})-\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}w_{0},


we calculate that




\displaystyle{\mathrm{d}}Y_{t}(\xi_{0})

\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{D}}Y_{t}(\xi_{0})\;\!\mathrm{d}t+\Sigma\,\;\!\mathrm{d}B_{t}.\qed

3.2 Derivation of the coarse-grained equations


With the characterisation of the projected stochastic process Y=Y(\eta_{0}) of Lemma 3.2, we
can now derive the coarse-grained system, i.e., the evolution in (z,w).


Theorem 3.3.

Consider the setup of Section 2, including the Compression Property 1.2.

1. 

For z_{0}\in{\mathbf{Z}} and w_{0}\in{\mathbf{W}} consider (z_{t},\eta_{t})={\mathbb{U}}_{t}(z_{0},w_{0}) as in part 1 of Theorem 2.5.
Then the pair (z_{t},w_{t}:={\mathbb{P}}\eta_{t}) satisfies the ODE in {\mathbf{Z}}{\times}{\mathbf{W}}




\displaystyle\dot{z}_{t}
\displaystyle={\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z_{t})({\mathrm{D}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z_{t})+{\mathsf{C}}^{*}w_{t})

(3.2a)


\displaystyle\dot{w}_{t}
\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{D}}(w_{t}+{\mathsf{C}}z_{t}).

(3.2b)


2. 

For z_{0}\in{\mathbf{Z}}, w_{0}\in{\mathbf{W}}, and \xi_{0}\sim\widehat{\mathbb{Q}}_{\#}\gamma_{\beta}, consider (z_{t},\eta_{t})={\mathbb{U}}_{t}(z_{0},w_{0}+\xi_{0}) as in part 3 of Theorem 2.5. Set w_{t}:=\widehat{\mathbb{P}}\eta_{t}.
Then the pair (z_{t},w_{t}) satisfies the SDE




\displaystyle{\mathrm{d}}z_{t}
\displaystyle={\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z_{t})({\mathrm{D}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z_{t})+{\mathsf{C}}^{*}w_{t}){\mathrm{d}}t

(3.3a)


\displaystyle{\mathrm{d}}w_{t}
\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{D}}(w_{t}+{\mathsf{C}}z_{t})\;\!\mathrm{d}t+\Sigma\,\;\!\mathrm{d}B_{t},

(3.3b)

where \Sigma is a square root of ({\mathbb{D}}+{\mathbb{D}}^{*})/\beta, and (z_{t},w_{t})|_{t=0}=(z_{0},w_{0}). Here B_{t} is a standard {\mathbf{W}}-valued Brownian motion.

3. 

Similarly, if (z_{0},\eta_{0})\sim\mu_{\beta} and (z_{t},\eta_{t})={\mathbb{U}}_{t}(z_{0},\eta_{0}), then (z_{t},w_{t}) is a stationary solution of the SDE (3.3). The single-time marginal is




\nu_{\beta}({\mathrm{d}}z\;\!\mathrm{d}w):=(\pi_{z,w})_{\#}\mu_{\beta}({\mathrm{d}}z\;\!\mathrm{d}w)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(*)}}{{=}}\mu_{\beta,{\mathbf{Z}}}({\mathrm{d}}z){\mathcal{N}}_{\mathbf{W}}(-{\mathsf{C}}z,\beta^{-1})({\mathrm{d}}w)

(3.4)

(and this measure is therefore invariant under the SDE (3.3)). It can alternatively be written as




\nu_{\beta}({\mathrm{d}}z\;\!\mathrm{d}w)=\frac{1}{Z_{\beta}}\exp\Big[-\beta\Big({\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)+\tfrac{1}{2}\|w\|_{{\mathbf{H}}}^{2}+\left({\mathsf{C}}z\middle|w\right)_{\mathbf{H}}^{2}\Big)\Big]\;\!\mathrm{d}z\;\!\mathrm{d}w.

(3.5)






Remark 3.4.

From here onward the implicit probability space will be always the same as in
Lemma 2.4 and Theorem 2.5, namely ({\mathbf{X}},{\mathcal{B}}({\mathbf{X}})_{\gamma_{\beta}},\gamma_{\beta}).
 ∎



Remark 3.5.

This coarse-graining approach is similar to many approaches in the Mori-Zwanzig style, but nonetheless different; we comment on this in Section 5.1.

Remark 3.6 (Invariance of \nu_{\beta}).

The invariance of the measure in (3.5) can also be seen by explicit computation. The generator
associated with the stochastic process (3.3) is




\mathcal{L}={\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)\big({\mathrm{D}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)+{\mathsf{C}}^{*}w\big)\cdot\nabla_{z}-{\mathbb{D}}(w+{\mathsf{C}}z)\cdot\nabla_{w}+\frac{1}{\beta}{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{sym}}}\,{:}\nabla^{2}_{w},


with adjoint operator




\mathcal{L}^{\star}\rho=-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{z}\big[\rho{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)({\mathrm{D}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z){+}{\mathsf{C}}^{*}w)\big]+\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}\big[\rho{\mathbb{D}}(w+{\mathsf{C}}z)\big]+\frac{1}{\beta}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}\big[\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}(\rho{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{sym}}})\big].


To show that \nu_{\beta} is invariant, we show that {\mathcal{L}}^{\star}\nu_{\beta}=0. Identifying \nu_{\beta} with its Lebesgue density, note that




\nabla_{z}\nu_{\beta}=-\beta\nu_{\beta}({\mathrm{D}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)+{\mathsf{C}}^{*}w),\qquad\nabla_{w}\nu_{\beta}=-\beta\nu_{\beta}(w{+}{\mathsf{C}}z),\\
\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{1}{\beta}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}(\nu_{\beta}{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{sym}}})=-{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{sym}}}\nabla_{w}\nu_{\beta}.


We then calculate




\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{z}\big[\nu_{\beta}{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)({\mathrm{D}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z){+}{\mathsf{C}}^{*}w)\big]
\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\beta}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{z}\big[{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)\nabla_{z}\nu_{\beta}\big]




\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\beta}\underbrace{\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{z}\big[{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z)\big]}_{\text{$=0$ by assumption}}\!\!\cdot\nabla_{z}\nu_{\beta}-\frac{1}{\beta}\underbrace{{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}(z){:}\nabla_{z}^{2}\nu_{\beta}}_{\text{$=0$ by ${\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{*}=-{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{A}}$}}=0,


and




\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}\left[\nu_{\beta}{\mathbb{D}}(w{+}{\mathsf{C}}z)+\frac{1}{\beta}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}(\nu_{\beta}{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{sym}}})\right]
\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}\left[-\frac{1}{\beta}{\mathbb{D}}\nabla_{w}\nu_{\beta}+\frac{1}{\beta}{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{sym}}}\nabla_{w}\nu_{\beta}\right]




\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\beta}\underbrace{\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\nolimits_{w}\left[{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{skw}}}\nabla_{w}\nu_{\beta}\right]}_{\text{$=0$ by ${{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{skw}}^{*}}=-{{\mathbb{D}}_{\mathrm{skw}}}$}}=0.


Therefore \nu_{\beta} is invariant.


For a harmonic potential V, existence of an invariant measure can be shown using controllability as
in [JPS17].

4.3 Reformulation in GENERIC form


We now re-interpret the ODE (3.2) and the SDE (3.3) as GENERIC equations as introduced in the previous sections; for this we need to enlarge the state space.


We saw above that in GENERIC ODEs and SDEs the energy {\mathcal{E}} is (almost surely) constant. The total energy {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{total}} in (2.1) is a natural candidate for such an energy, but it has two drawbacks: first, it depends on \eta, to which we do not have access after coarse-graining, and secondly, in the case of the SDE the energy {\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{total}} is almost surely infinite (see Remark 2.2).

Appendix C Dilations


The notion of dilations and compressions was introduced in Section 3.1.
We now recall the existence of dilations.


Theorem C.1 ([SzF70, Thm. 8.1]).

Every strongly continuous contraction semigroup (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} on a Hilbert space {\mathbf{G}} admits a
dilation (S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} on a Hilbert space {\mathbf{H}}\supset{\mathbf{G}}.


Moreover, there is a minimal dilation in the sense that




\mathrm{span}\Big(\bigcup\nolimits_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}S_{t}{\mathbf{G}}\Big)\ \text{ is dense in \ }{\mathbf{H}}.


Any two minimal dilations \big({\mathbf{H}},(S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) and \big(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}},(\widetilde{S}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big)
are isormorphic in the sense that there exists a Hilbert-space isomorphism \Psi\colon{\mathbf{H}}\to\widetilde{\mathbf{H}} such
that \widetilde{S}_{t}=\Psi S_{t}\Psi^{-1} for all t\in{\mathbb{R}}.



It turns out that even for finite-dimensional {\mathbf{G}} the dilation space {\mathbf{H}}
will be infinite-dimensional as soon as (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} is not unitary, i.e.,
as soon as C_{t} is a non-trivial contraction. Moreover, the subspace {\mathbf{G}}
cannot be contained in the domain of the generator of the unitary group
(S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}, as we now show.


Remark C.2 (Domains of the generators).

The unitary group has a densely-defined generator
{\mathbb{J}}\colon\mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}})\subset{\mathbf{H}}\to{\mathbf{H}} which is skew-adjoint,
i.e., {\mathbb{J}}^{*}=-{\mathbb{J}}. For h_{0}\in\mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}}) the function
h(t)=S_{t}h_{0}=\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}}{h_{0}} is differentiable and satisfies
\dot{h}(t)={\mathbb{J}}h(t).


The contraction semigroup can be written as C_{t}=\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}} for a
generator {\mathbb{D}} satisfying {\mathbb{D}}+{\mathbb{D}}^{*}\geq 0. If C_{t} is not unitary,
then {\mathbb{D}} is not skew-adjoint and there exists a g\in{\mathbf{G}} such that
\gamma:=\left(g\middle|{\mathbb{D}}{g}\right)_{\mathbf{G}}>0. We set p(t)=\|\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}g\|^{2} and find
\lim_{t\to 0^{+}}\dot{p}(t)=-2\gamma. Assuming g\in\mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}}), the
dilation property gives
\dot{p}(0)=\frac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}t}\|{\mathbb{P}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}}g\|^{2}\big|_{t=0}=2\left({\mathbb{P}}g\middle|{\mathbb{P}}{\mathbb{J}}g\right)_{\mathbf{H}}=2\left(g\middle|{\mathbb{J}}g\right)_{\mathbf{H}}=0. This is a
contradiction, and we conclude g\not\in\mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}}).


Hence, {\mathbb{J}} is an unbounded operator, and {\mathbf{H}} is
infinite-dimensional. If \left(g\middle|{\mathbb{D}}g\right)_{\mathbf{G}}>0 for every g\not=0, then
we even have \mathrm{dom}({\mathbb{J}})\cap{\mathbf{G}}=\{0\}.
 ∎



In the context of this paper, it is advantageous to generalize the notion of dilation slightly.


Definition C.3 (Generalized dilation).

A triple \big({\mathbf{H}},\Phi,(S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) is called a generalized dilation of the contraction
semigroup \big({\mathbf{W}},(\widehat{C}_{t})_{t\geq 0}\big) if (S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} is a strongly continuous unitary group on {\mathbf{H}}
and the linear map \Phi\colon{\mathbf{W}}\to{\mathbf{H}} satisfies




\Phi^{*}\Phi=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{W}}\quad\text{and}\quad\Phi^{*}S_{t}\Phi=\widehat{C}_{t}\in\mathrm{Lin}({\mathbf{W}};{\mathbf{W}})\text{ \ for all }t\geq 0.





Note that from this definition we see that {\mathbb{P}}=\Phi\Phi^{*}\colon{\mathbf{H}}\to{\mathbf{H}} is an orthogonal projection
onto {\mathbf{G}}=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}\subset{\mathbf{H}}. In particular, setting C_{t}=\Phi\widehat{C}_{t}\Phi^{*}|_{\mathbf{G}} the unitary
group \big({\mathbf{H}},(S_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) is a dilation of \big({\mathbf{G}},(C_{t})_{t\geq 0}\big) in the sense of
Definition 3.1. However, since \Phi\colon{\mathbf{W}}\to{\mathbf{G}} is an isometry with inverse
\Phi^{*}|_{\mathbf{G}}, the two contraction semigroups (C_{t})_{t\geq 0} and (\widehat{C}_{t})_{t\geq 0} are isomorphic. As
a consequence, all minimal dilations are isomorphic to any minimal generalized dilation, which is defined via
the minimality condition that \bigcup_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\Phi\big(C_{t}{\mathbf{W}}\big) is dense in {\mathbf{H}}.


C.1 An explicit construction of a generalized dilation


Here we repeat the explicit construction of a generalized dilation from [LaS89, Thm. 2.1]
or [KüS84, Sec. 1.2.3] and give the full proofs because of its importance of compressions and dilations for our analysis.


We now write the contraction semigroup \big({\mathbf{W}},(C_{t})_{t\geq 0}\big) in the form C_{t}=\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}. Moreover, we follow our assumptions in Section 2 and assume




\mathrm{dim}({\mathbf{W}})<\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\exists\,\delta>0:\ \|\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}}\|\leq\mathrm{e}^{-\delta t}\text{ for all }t\geq 0.

(C.1)

To construct a generalized dilation we define




\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}:={\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})\text{ with }\|f\|_{{\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}}}^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\|f(y)\|_{\mathbf{W}}^{2}\;\!\mathrm{d}y\quad\text{and}\quad{\mathbf{G}}:=\big\{\,\Phi v\in\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\>\big|\>v\in{\mathbf{W}}\,\big\},


where the bounded linear operator \Phi\colon{\mathbf{W}}\to{\mathbf{G}}\subset\overline{{\mathbf{H}}} is given by




(\Phi w)(y):=\Sigma_{\mathbb{D}}\,\mathrm{e}^{y{\mathbb{D}}}w\,\bm{1}_{{]{-}\infty,0]}}(y),\quad\text{with }\Sigma_{\mathbb{D}}:=({\mathbb{D}}{+}{\mathbb{D}}^{*})^{1/2},

(C.2)

with adjoint operator \Phi^{*}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\to{\mathbf{W}},

\big(\overline{{\mathbf{H}}},\Phi,({\mathbb{S}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) is a generalized dilation for
\big({\mathbf{W}},(\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}})_{t\geq 0}\big).


Proposition C.4 (Explicit dilation).

{\mathbb{P}}=\Phi\Phi^{*}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\to{\mathbf{G}}\subset\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}.

inverse \Phi^{*}|_{\mathbf{G}}. Moreover, {\mathbb{P}} is the orthogonal projector from \overline{{\mathbf{H}}} onto {\mathbf{G}}.

Defining the strongly continuous unitary shift group ({\mathbb{S}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} on \overline{{\mathbf{H}}}={\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})

Choosing N\in{\mathbb{N}} sufficiently big, the last term is less than \varepsilon^{2}/4, and thus we conclude
\|f-\widehat{f}_{N}\|_{{\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})}<\varepsilon as desired. Hence, \mathfrak{G} is dense in
\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}={\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}}).
 ∎




C.2 Continuous extension of the group (\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} from {\mathbf{H}} to {\mathbf{X}}


In Assumption 2.3 we assumed that the unitary group
\big({\mathbf{H}},(\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) describing the heat bath can be
extended to a strongly continuous group on the larger space {\mathbf{X}}, on which we
are able to realize the Gaussian measure \gamma_{\beta} for the
finite-temperature heat bath. We will show in Proposition C.6
that this assumption is already a consequence of the dilation property from
Assumption 1.2.


As a first step we construct the Gaussian measure \overline{\gamma}_{\beta} on an
extension \overline{{\mathbf{X}}} of the special space \overline{{\mathbf{H}}}={\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}}). This leads
to a classical white noise process, but now taking values in the
finite-dimensional Hilbert space {\mathbf{W}}. While translations {\mathbb{S}}_{t} can easily
defined for the white noise process, we have to be more careful and construct a
Hilbert space \overline{{\mathbf{X}}} on which we can extend the unitary group
\big(\overline{{\mathbf{H}}},({\mathbb{S}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) to a strongly continuous group
\big(\overline{{\mathbf{X}}},({\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big), which will be no longer
unitary. If {\mathbb{N}}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{X}}} is the embedding operator, then the
extension property means




\forall\>t\in{\mathbb{R}}\ \ \forall\>h\in\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}:\quad{\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t}{\mathbb{N}}h={\mathbb{N}}{\mathbb{S}}_{t}h.

(C.5)

As explained in Section 2.2 we further
need that {\mathbb{C}}={\mathbb{N}}{\mathbb{N}}^{*}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{X}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{X}}} is trace class.


We give an explicit construction following the ideas in [Rey06]. We
define the self-adjoint operator
{\mathbb{A}}\colon\mathrm{Dom}({\mathbb{A}})\subset\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{H}}} via





\displaystyle\mathrm{Dom}({\mathbb{A}})=\big\{\,u\in{\mathrm{H}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})\>\big|\>t\mapsto(1{+}t^{2})u(t)\in{\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})\,\big\},




\displaystyle({\mathbb{A}}u)(t)=-\frac{1}{2}u^{\prime\prime}(t)+\frac{t^{2}}{2}\,u(t).


Here {\mathrm{H}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}}) is the Sobolev space of measurable {\mathrm{L}}^{2}-functions
u\colon{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbf{W}} with two weak derivatives in {\mathrm{L}}^{2}. This is a {\mathbf{W}}-valued
version of the quantum harmonic oscillator, and hence is self-adjoint with the
discrete spectrum \big\{\,n{-}1/2\>\big|\>n\in{\mathbb{N}}\,\big\}\subset{[1/2,\infty)}, where
all eigenvalues have multiplicity \dim({\mathbf{W}})<\infty. Consequently {\mathbb{A}} is
an invertible operator, and its inverse {\mathbb{A}}^{-1} is a Hilbert-Schmidt
operator. This implies that {\mathbb{A}} satisfies the assumptions for the
construction in Section A.2, i.e. we can define




\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}=\mathrm{Dom}({\mathbb{A}})={\mathrm{H}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})\cap{\mathrm{L}}^{2}_{(2)}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})\quad\text{and}\quad\overline{{\mathbf{X}}}=\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}^{*}={\mathrm{H}}^{-2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}})+{\mathrm{L}}^{2}_{(-2)}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}}),


where the subscripts “(m)” denote the {\mathrm{L}}^{2} space with measure
(1{+}t^{2})^{m}{\mathrm{d}}t. In \overline{{\mathbf{V}}} we choose the graph norm \|u\|_{\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}}=\|{\mathbb{A}}u\|_{\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}}.


Concerning the shift group (\overline{{\mathbf{H}}},{\mathbb{S}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}} we observe that it can be
restricted to \overline{{\mathbf{V}}}, since u\in\overline{{\mathbf{V}}} implies {\mathbb{S}}_{t}u\in\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}
for all t. Setting {\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{V}}_{t}={\mathbb{S}}_{t}|_{\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}}:\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{V}}} we
have




\displaystyle\|{\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{V}}_{t}u\|_{\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}}
\displaystyle\leq C\big(\|({{\mathbb{S}}}_{t}u)^{\prime\prime}\|_{{\mathrm{L}}^{2}}+\|(1{+}s^{2})({{\mathbb{S}}}_{t}u)(s)\|_{{\mathrm{L}}^{2}}\big)




\displaystyle\leq 2C\big(\|u^{\prime\prime}\|_{{\mathrm{L}}^{2}}+(1{+}t^{2})\|(1{+}r^{2})u(r)\|_{{\mathrm{L}}^{2}}\big)\leq(1{+}t^{2})C\|u\|_{\overline{{\mathbf{V}}}}.


Hence, \big(\overline{{\mathbf{V}}},({\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{V}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) forms a strongly continuous group of shift
operators. By dualization (with respect to the duality in \overline{{\mathbf{H}}}) we can define the extension




{\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{X}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{X}}};\ \ {\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t}=\big({\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{V}}_{-t}\big)^{*}


which provides the strongly continuous group \big(\overline{{\mathbf{X}}},({\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) satisfying \|{\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t}\|_{\overline{{\mathbf{X}}}}\leq C^{2}(1{+}t^{2}).


Proposition C.6 (Assumption 2.3 holds).

If the contraction semigroup \big({\mathbf{G}},(\mathrm{e}^{-t{\mathbb{D}}})_{t\geq 0}\big)
satisfies (C.1) and
\big({\mathbf{H}},(\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) is an arbitrary minimal
dilation, then there exists a larger space {\mathbf{X}} with embedding
{\mathbb{N}}:{\mathbf{H}}\to{\mathbf{X}} and a strongly continuous group (\widehat{S}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}
such





\displaystyle{\mathbb{N}}{\mathbb{N}}^{*}\colon{\mathbf{X}}\to{\mathbf{X}}\quad\text{is trace class}




\displaystyle\forall\,t\in{\mathbb{R}}\ \forall\,h\in{\mathbf{H}}:\quad\widehat{S}_{t}{\mathbb{N}}h={\mathbb{N}}\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}h.





Proof.

We use the explicit construction of the generalized dilation
\big(\overline{{\mathbf{H}}},({\mathbb{S}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big) and of the explicit extension to
\big(\overline{{\mathbf{X}}},({\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t})_{t\in{\mathbb{R}}}\big).


By Theorem C.1 the two dilations are unitarily equivalent by a
unitary map U\colon{\mathbf{H}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}. If \overline{{\mathbb{N}}} is the embedding of \overline{{\mathbf{H}}}
into \overline{{\mathbf{X}}}, then we can define




{\mathbf{X}}:=\overline{{\mathbf{X}}},\quad{\mathbb{N}}:=\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}\,U,\quad\widehat{S}_{t}={\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t}.


Clearly, {\mathbb{N}}{\mathbb{N}}^{*}=\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}U\,U^{*}\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}^{*}=\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}\,\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}^{*} is
trace class by the explicit construction. Moreover,




\widehat{S}_{t}{\mathbb{N}}h={\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t}\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}Uh\overset{\text{(1)}}{=}\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}{\mathbb{S}}_{t}Uh=\overline{{\mathbb{N}}}\,UU^{-1}{\mathbb{S}}_{t}Uh\overset{\text{(2)}}{=}{\mathbb{N}}\,\mathrm{e}^{t{\mathbb{J}}_{\mathcal{B}}}h


holds for all h\in{\mathbf{H}}. In \overset{\text{(1)}}{=} we used the explicit
extension of {\mathbb{S}}^{\mathbf{X}}_{t} of {\mathbb{S}}_{t} with embedding \overline{{\mathbb{N}}}, and in
\overset{\text{(2)}}{=} we used the definition of {\mathbb{N}} and that the two
dilations are equivalent via the unitary operator U.
∎



The advantage of using the explicit generalized dilation involving
\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}={\mathrm{L}}^{2}({\mathbb{R}};{\mathbf{W}}) becomes even more apparent if we use the structure of
the mapping \Phi\colon{\mathbf{W}}\to{\mathbf{G}}\subset\overline{{\mathbf{H}}} and
\Phi^{*}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\to{\mathbf{W}}. Combining \Phi^{*} and the shift {\mathbb{S}}_{t} we
obtain the mapping




{\mathcal{U}}:\overline{{\mathbf{H}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{H}}};\quad({\mathcal{U}}f)(t):=\Phi^{*}\big({\mathbb{S}}_{t}f\big).


This corresponds to the mapping t\mapsto Y_{t}(\eta_{0}):=\widehat{\mathbb{P}}\widehat{S}_{t}\eta_{0} from Lemma 2.4. We simply “dropped” the Hilbert-space
isomorphism \Phi:{\mathbf{W}}\overset{1\text{-}1}{\longleftrightarrow}{\mathbf{G}}.


We now show that {\mathcal{U}} has a bounded linear extension \widehat{\mathcal{U}}\colon\overline{{\mathbf{X}}}\to\overline{{\mathbf{X}}} that is consistent with Y_{t} in Lemma 2.4
and is defined everywhere, i.e., we do not need the measurable extension
\widehat{\mathbb{P}} defined \gamma_{\beta} a.e.
For this we observe that




\big({\mathcal{U}}f\big)(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}\Sigma_{\mathbb{D}}\,\mathrm{e}^{s{\mathbb{D}}^{*}}f(s{-}t)\;\!\mathrm{d}s.


Thus, {\mathcal{U}} is realized by convolution with the kernel s\mapsto\Sigma_{\mathbb{D}}\,\mathrm{e}^{s{\mathbb{D}}^{*}}\bm{1}_{]-\infty,0]}. In Fourier space the
convolution is realized by the multiplication with the Fourier multiplier




{\mathbb{R}}\ni\sigma\mapsto M(\sigma)^{*}:=\Sigma_{\mathbb{D}}\big({\mathbb{D}}^{*}-\mathrm{i}\sigma{\mathbb{I}}\big)^{-1}


which is smooth and bounded. As the operator {\mathbb{A}} stays invariant (up to
changing constants) under Fourier transform \mathfrak{F}, we also see that
\mathfrak{F} maps {{\mathbf{V}}} into itself, and hence by duality also {{\mathbf{X}}} into
{{\mathbf{X}}}. Clearly, multiplying by M defines a bounded linear operator in
{{\mathbf{V}}}, because M lies in {\mathrm{C}}^{2}_{\mathrm{b}}\big({\mathbb{R}};\mathrm{Lin}({\mathbf{W}})\big). By
duality the multiplication multiplying by M^{*} defines a bounded linear
operator in {{\mathbf{X}}}={{\mathbf{V}}}^{*}. This shows that there is a bounded linear extension
\widehat{\mathcal{U}}\colon{{\mathbf{X}}}\to{{\mathbf{X}}} of {\mathcal{U}}\colon{{\mathbf{H}}}\to{{\mathbf{H}}}.
